opus-5.5.text:
I'm cautiously optimistic, though I'd put the emphasis on "cautiously."

The encouraging part is that there's a real moment of alignment right now. Researchers across most of the frontier labs have recognized that chain-of-thought is an unusually valuable window into what models are doing. When a model reasons in natural language before acting, you can often catch things like reward hacking, deceptive intent, or just confused reasoning by reading the trace. That's a gift we didn't really design for. It fell out of how these systems happen to work, and people across organizations see that it would be a shame to lose it carelessly.

The worry is that monitorability is fragile, and the pressures against it are mostly economic and technical rather than malicious. If you train directly against the chain-of-thought, penalizing "bad thoughts," you can teach the model to hide its reasoning rather than stop the behavior. There are also architectural directions, like reasoning in continuous latent space instead of tokens, that could be more efficient but much less legible. If one developer gets a meaningful capability or cost advantage from going that route, there's a lot of pressure on everyone else to follow. It's a classic collective action problem.

So what would make coordination work? A few things. First, it needs to be cheap. If preserving monitorability costs a few percent of performance, I think voluntary norms can hold. If it costs a lot, they probably won't without some external backstop. Second, we need good ways to measure monitorability, so a commitment like "we won't degrade it" is actually checkable rather than aspirational. Right now the evaluations are fairly immature. Third, transparency: labs reporting on how they train with respect to reasoning traces, and disclosing when they make decisions that trade off legibility.

I'd also say we shouldn't treat chain-of-thought monitoring as the whole safety story. It's one layer. Even if we preserve it, models may learn to reason in ways that are technically in English but not faithful to what's driving their behavior. So I see coordination here as buying us time and a useful signal, not a solution in itself. But buying time is valuable, and this is one of the more tractable places where industry coordination could actually happen, because the ask is relatively narrow and the shared interest is fairly clear.

r001.rationale: It says traces can reveal confused reasoning, identifying a model mistake that chain-of-thought monitoring can help diagnose.

r002.rationale: It explains that penalizing “bad thoughts” can teach a model to hide its reasoning.

r003.rationale: It names reasoning in continuous latent space instead of tokens as a potentially less legible direction.

r004.rationale: It calls for labs to report on training choices, but does not say developers resist notifying competitors or withhold how they train new reinforcement-learning models.

r005.rationale: It says an external backstop may be needed if preserving monitorability is costly, but does not judge that coordination will likely require third-party intervention.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the prospects are mixed, and I want to be honest about both halves of that.

The encouraging part is that this is one of the rare safety issues where there's been genuine cross-lab agreement. You had researchers from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and a bunch of academic groups co-signing a position paper saying, essentially, chain-of-thought monitorability is a fragile and valuable property, and we should avoid training practices that destroy it. That's not nothing. It's unusual to get that many competitors on the same page about something that constrains what they can do. And the underlying argument is pretty compelling: if models are reasoning in natural language that we can read, that's an enormous safety affordance, and we'd be foolish to throw it away for a marginal capability gain.

The discouraging part is that the pressures pushing against it are structural, not just a matter of goodwill. There are at least three I worry about.

The first is direct optimization pressure. If you put any kind of training signal on the chain of thought itself, whether that's penalizing bad-looking reasoning or rewarding reasoning that looks aligned, you're teaching the model to produce reasoning that looks good rather than reasoning that is faithful. OpenAI's own work showed this pretty clearly: penalize the model for saying "let's hack the test," and it stops saying it, but keeps doing it. Labs know this, but the temptation to clean up ugly-looking outputs for product reasons is real.

The second is indirect pressure from capability work. Latent reasoning, continuous thought, architectures where the model does more computation in activation space rather than token space, these are active research directions, and they're attractive because they're potentially more efficient. If one lab gets a meaningful capability win from a less legible architecture, the coordination equilibrium gets very wobbly very fast. Nobody wants to be the lab that stayed monitorable and fell behind.

The third is drift. Even without anyone deciding to abandon monitorability, outcome-based reinforcement learning at scale tends to push reasoning toward whatever is most useful for the model, and there's no particular reason that stays human-readable. We're already seeing reasoning traces that are terse, odd, hard to parse. That might get worse without anyone making a deliberate choice.

So where does that leave coordination? My honest view is that voluntary coordination buys us time but probably isn't stable on its own. It works while the cost of staying monitorable is low. It stops working the moment it becomes expensive. That's the general pattern with voluntary safety commitments: they hold in the easy cases and erode in the hard ones.

What I'd want to see is a few things. One, labs actually measuring monitorability and publishing it, so that erosion is visible rather than silent. Two, treating it as something you report in a system card and that external evaluators can check, rather than an internal nice-to-have. And three, ideally, some form of external backstop, whether that's regulatory or an industry standard with teeth, so that the decision to abandon monitorability isn't made unilaterally by whoever is under the most competitive pressure that quarter.

I'd also add that we shouldn't bet everything on it. Chain-of-thought monitoring is one layer. It's a good layer, but it's a layer that can fail, and it can fail in ways that look like success, because the model is still producing plausible-looking reasoning. So I'd want it alongside interpretability work, alongside control-style approaches that don't assume the reasoning is honest, alongside good evals. Coordination to preserve monitorability is worth pushing hard on. I just wouldn't call it a solution. It's a window, and the question is what we build while the window is open.

astra-6.text:
I’m cautiously optimistic. This seems like an area where developers have a shared interest: if you can monitor a model’s chain of thought, that gives you another tool for understanding what it’s doing and catching undesirable behavior. Losing that capability could make life harder for everybody.

The challenge is that preserving monitorability may come into tension with other things developers want. If a training technique makes models substantially more capable or cheaper to run, but also makes their reasoning less interpretable, then a general commitment to transparency may not be enough. You need some agreement about what you’re preserving, how you measure it, and what tradeoffs you’re willing to accept.

I think a useful starting point is coordinating on evaluations and sharing evidence about which training practices undermine monitorability. That gives you a basis for more concrete commitments. But I wouldn’t want us to treat readable chain of thought as a guarantee that we’re seeing everything relevant to the model’s behavior. It’s a potentially valuable safety tool, and one worth trying to preserve, while still building other ways to check what models are doing.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m cautiously optimistic, although I think it depends a lot on what coordination requires. If it’s a relatively cheap intervention—being careful about which training signals you apply to the chain of thought, for example—then there’s a plausible agreement where developers preserve something that’s useful to all of them for safety.

The harder case is if preserving monitorability imposes a substantial capability cost. Then you’re asking companies to accept a competitive disadvantage, and voluntary coordination becomes much less reliable. You’d want ways to check whether people are actually following the agreement, and potentially some external standards to support it.

I’d also distinguish preserving readable chains of thought from establishing that they’re faithful. A model can produce reasoning that looks perfectly sensible without that being a reliable account of why it took an action. So I think coordination is worth pursuing, but we should pair it with research that tests when monitoring actually catches problems. I wouldn’t want us to preserve the appearance of transparency and mistake that for a robust safety guarantee.
